cards.b: The removal of waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements.
The maintenance of a constant internal environment.
The normal value of a controlled factor, e.g. about 37 °C for human body temperature.
A change from the set point is detected and a response returns the factor towards the set point; the response then switches off.

cards.f: Blood glucose too high: what happens?
cards.b: Pancreas detects it and secretes insulin; the liver converts glucose to glycogen; blood glucose falls to the set point.

cards.f: Blood glucose too low: what happens?
cards.b: Pancreas secretes glucagon; the liver converts glycogen to glucose; blood glucose rises to the set point.

cards.f: Which organ makes insulin and glucagon, and which is the target?
cards.b: The pancreas secretes both. The target organ is the liver.

cards.f: Role of the brain in temperature control
cards.b: Monitors blood temperature (and skin receptor impulses) and coordinates responses to keep temperature near the set point.

cards.f: Role of skin receptors and sensory neurones
cards.b: Receptors detect temperature; sensory neurones carry impulses to the brain.

cards.f: Response when the body is too hot
cards.b: Sweating (evaporation removes heat), vasodilation of arterioles (more heat lost), hairs lie flat.

cards.f: Response when the body is too cold
cards.b: Shivering (respiration releases heat), vasoconstriction of arterioles (less heat lost), hairs stand up trapping insulating air, no sweating.
Vasodilation: arterioles to skin capillaries widen. Vasoconstriction: they narrow. Capillaries themselves do not move.

cards.f: How do sweat glands cool the body?
cards.b: Sweat evaporates from the skin surface, transferring heat energy away.

cards.f: How does shivering warm the body?
cards.b: Rapid involuntary muscle contractions increase respiration, which releases heat.
Fatty tissue under the skin and a layer of air trapped by raised hairs reduce heat loss.

short.q: Explain how the body responds when blood glucose concentration rises after a meal. [3]
short.model: The pancreas secretes insulin into the blood, which causes the liver to convert glucose to glycogen, so blood glucose falls to the set point.

short.q: Explain why blood glucose control is an example of negative feedback. [2]
short.model: A change away from the set point causes a response that brings the glucose concentration back towards the set point.
points: response reverses the change / returns to set point

short.q: Describe how vasodilation helps to cool the body. [3]
short.model: Arterioles supplying skin capillaries widen, so more blood flows near the skin surface and more heat is lost to the surroundings.
points: more blood through skin surface capillaries

short.q: A student says that blood vessels move closer to the skin surface when hot. Explain what is wrong. [2]
short.model: Vessels do not move. Arterioles widen (vasodilation) so more blood flows through the capillaries near the surface.
points: arterioles widen to increase blood flow near surface

short.q: Explain how shivering and hair erector muscles help a person who is cold. [3]
short.model: Shivering contracts muscles rapidly, increasing respiration and releasing heat. Hair erector muscles raise hairs, trapping an insulating layer of air.
